name: Leading Inclusive Teams
objectives: For a team you lead or know, identify the signs of belonging and choose one habit that builds it, naming a habit you can repeat every week

Given a real decision about people, apply a bias check: set criteria first, write your reasons and ask whether you would decide the same for someone from a different group, before the decision is final
Given a job opening or promotion, plan fair hiring or promotion habits such as job-related requirements and structured interviews, judging every candidate by the same job-related standards
For a regular team meeting, plan a meeting routine that gives every person a fair chance to speak, including at least two tools such as going around, silent writing or asking remote people first
For one part of your team's work, choose one accessibility improvement and use respectful language for names and pronouns, handling requests privately

When someone reports or you see exclusion or harassment, list the steps you will follow, who you will tell and where the official rules are, acting right away and protecting the person from retaliation

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What belonging looks like on a team
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the signs of belonging on a team and pick one habit that builds it.
This lesson builds toward: For a team you lead or know, you will identify the signs of belonging and choose one habit that builds it, naming a habit you can repeat every week.
A team has belonging when every person feels respected, safe to speak up, and valued for what they bring. People who feel they belong share ideas, admit mistakes early and stay longer. People who feel left out go quiet, and the team loses their ideas.
Belonging is built by small, repeated actions from the leader: learning how to say each person's name correctly, sharing important information with everyone at the same time, giving stretch tasks fairly, and thanking people for raising problems instead of punishing them.
Ask, do not guess. A short, private question like "What would make it easier for you to speak up here?" tells you more than any assumption.
Step by step:
- Notice who speaks up and who stays quiet.
- Share key information with everyone at the same time.
- Spread good assignments fairly.
- Thank people who raise problems.
- Ask privately what would help each person speak up.
Words to know:
- Inclusion: making sure every person can take part fully and fairly.
- Belonging: the feeling of being respected and valued as part of a group.
- Psychological safety: the shared belief that you can speak up, ask questions or admit mistakes without being punished or mocked.
Try it now: For one week, notice who speaks in your team meetings and who does not. Write down one belonging habit from this lesson you will start, and one person you will ask privately what would help them speak up.
You can now describe what belonging looks like and start one habit that builds it.

check.q: What happens when people on a team feel left out?
options: They work harder to prove themselves
They go quiet and the team loses their ideas
Nothing changes
They always leave that day
check.why: People who feel left out go quiet, and their ideas are lost.

check.q: You are not sure why a team member never speaks in meetings. What would you do?
options: Ask them privately what would make it easier to speak up
Assume they have nothing to say
Call on them first in front of everyone
Ask the rest of the team about them
check.why: Ask, do not guess; a short private question tells you more.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Spotting unconscious bias
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a simple check to catch bias in a real decision.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real decision about people, you will apply a bias check: set criteria first, write your reasons and ask whether you would decide the same for someone from a different group, before the decision is final.
Unconscious bias means quick judgments our brains make without our noticing, based on things like someone's age, accent, gender, race, disability, background or where they went to school. Everyone has them. Having them does not make you a bad person, but acting on them can lead to unfair decisions.
Common traps: liking people who remind us of ourselves (affinity bias), letting one good or bad trait color everything (the halo effect), and noticing only facts that fit what we already believe (confirmation bias).
You cannot remove bias by willpower alone, so build checks into decisions. Decide the criteria before you look at people. Write down your reasons. Ask: "Would I decide the same if this person were from a different group?" Get a second opinion on important calls.
Step by step:
- Write the criteria before you look at people or options.
- Judge each person against the same criteria.
- Write down the reason for your decision.
- Ask: "Would I decide the same if this person were from a different group?"
- Get a second opinion on big decisions.
Words to know:
- Unconscious bias: a quick judgment about people that we make without noticing.
- Affinity bias: favoring people who seem like us.
- Halo effect: letting one trait make us judge everything else about a person as good or bad.
- Criteria: the standards you use to make a decision.
Try it now: Think of a recent decision about people, like who got a shift, a project or a chance to speak. Write the criteria you should have used, then use the "would I decide the same?" question on it. Write one thing you would do differently.
You can now name common biases and use a simple check to make a fairer decision.

options: Favoring people like us
Judging everything by one trait
Noticing only facts that fit what we already believe
Confirming a meeting time
check.why: Confirmation bias filters facts to fit our existing view.

check.q: You are choosing who leads a new project. What would you do first?
options: Pick the person you get along with best
Decide the criteria before you look at people
Let the loudest person choose
Choose quickly and explain later
check.why: Deciding the criteria first is a check built into the decision.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Fair hiring and promotion habits
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set up a hiring or promotion process that judges everyone by the same job-related standards.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job opening or promotion, you will plan fair hiring or promotion habits such as job-related requirements and structured interviews, judging every candidate by the same job-related standards.
Fair hiring starts with the job, not the person. Write down what the job really needs and drop requirements that do not matter, like a degree for work that does not need one. Share openings widely, not only through friends of the current team.
Use structured interviews: ask every candidate the same job-related questions, score answers against the same scale, and have more than one person score. Do not ask about things that have nothing to do with the job, such as plans for children, religion or age.
For promotions, make the criteria known and give everyone a fair chance at the stretch work that leads to promotion. In the United States, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) enforces federal laws against job discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex (the EEOC says this includes pregnancy, sexual orientation and transgender status), national origin, age (40 or older), disability and genetic information. Whether a law covers your organization can depend on its size, so check eeoc.gov and talk to HR or an employment lawyer about your duties.
Step by step:
- List what the job truly needs; remove what it doesn't.
- Post the opening widely.
- Ask every candidate the same job-related questions.
- Score answers on the same scale, with more than one scorer.
- Make promotion criteria known and share stretch work fairly.
- Check eeoc.gov or ask HR about legal duties.
Words to know:
- Structured interview: an interview where every candidate gets the same questions and is scored the same way.
- EEOC: the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the federal agency that enforces laws against job discrimination.
- Protected characteristic: a trait, such as race, sex, age (40 or older) or disability, that the law says cannot be the basis of job decisions.
Official sources:
- EEOC: Employers
Try it now: Pick a real or pretend job on your team. Write three must-have requirements, remove one that is not really needed, and write three interview questions you would ask every candidate, with what a strong answer looks like.
You can now design a hiring or promotion process that treats every candidate by the same job-related standards and know where to check the law.

options: Each interviewer asks whatever they like
A chat over lunch
An interview with no scoring
Every candidate gets the same job-related questions, scored on the same scale
check.why: Same questions and the same scale help judge everyone fairly.

check.q: You want to share a new opening. What would you do?
options: Ask only the current team's friends
Share it widely, not only through friends of the team
Keep it quiet until you find someone
Post it only in one private group

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Running meetings where everyone is heard
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a meeting routine that gives every person a fair chance to speak.
This lesson builds toward: For a regular team meeting, you will plan a meeting routine that gives every person a fair chance to speak, including at least two tools such as going around, silent writing or asking remote people first.
In many meetings, a few people do most of the talking. That is not always because others have nothing to say. They may be newer, quieter, speaking a second language, joining remotely or used to being talked over.
Simple tools help: send the agenda ahead so people can prepare, go around the room, give a minute of silent writing before discussion, ask remote people first, and invite written ideas after the meeting.
Watch for interruptions and for people whose ideas get repeated by someone else and credited to them. Step in kindly: "Let's let Amina finish," or "That builds on what Luis said earlier." Rotate roles like note-taker so the same people do not always get the background tasks.
Step by step:
- Send the agenda ahead.
- Start with a go-around or a minute of silent writing.
- Call on remote people first.
- Stop interruptions kindly and credit ideas to the person who said them.
- Rotate the note-taker.
- Invite written ideas after the meeting.
Words to know:
- Go-around: giving every person a turn to speak, one by one.
- Hybrid meeting: a meeting where some people are in the room and some join online.
Try it now: Plan your next team meeting using at least three tools from this lesson. Write them on the agenda. After the meeting, note who spoke who usually does not.
You can now run a meeting that gives every person a fair chance to speak and be credited.

check.q: Why send the meeting agenda ahead?
options: So people can prepare
So the meeting can be longer
So no one needs to come
So the leader can skip planning
check.why: Preparing ahead helps quieter people and second-language speakers contribute.

check.q: The same two people always take notes. What would you do?
options: Leave it; they are good at it
Take notes yourself every time
Rotate the note-taker role
Stop taking notes
check.why: Rotating roles stops the same people from always getting background tasks.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Accessibility and respectful language
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make one part of your team's work more accessible and use respectful language.
This lesson builds toward: For one part of your team's work, you will choose one accessibility improvement and use respectful language for names and pronouns, handling requests privately.
Accessibility means people with disabilities, and everyone else, can use your workplace, documents, tools and meetings. Many disabilities cannot be seen. Simple steps help many people: captions on videos and online meetings, readable fonts and good contrast, documents that work with screen readers, step-free spaces, and quiet places to work.
Make it easy to ask for what someone needs, and handle requests privately. In the US, the Job Accommodation Network (askjan.org) gives free, confidential guidance on workplace accommodations, and the EEOC page for employers explains when denying a needed accommodation can be against the law.
Respectful language means calling people what they ask to be called: say names correctly, use the pronouns people share, and when unsure, ask politely or just use their name. Avoid jokes about someone's identity. If you get it wrong, apologize briefly, correct it and move on.
Step by step:
- Turn on captions in online meetings and videos.
- Use clear fonts, good contrast and headings in documents.
- Tell people how to ask for an accommodation, and keep requests private.
- Use the names and pronouns people share.
- If you get it wrong: apologize briefly, correct it, move on.
Words to know:
- Accessibility: designing places, tools and information so people with disabilities can use them.
- Accommodation: a change to a job or workplace that lets a person with a disability, a religious need or a pregnancy-related need do the work.
- Screen reader: software that reads screen text aloud for people who are blind or have low vision.
Official sources:
- Job Accommodation Network (JAN)
- EEOC: Employers
Try it now: Check one thing your team uses often, such as a sign-up form, a training video or the weekly meeting. List two accessibility fixes and do one of them this week.
You can now make team work more accessible, handle accommodation requests respectfully, and use respectful language.

check.q: Which is a simple accessibility step?
options: Using tiny fonts to fit more on a page
Playing videos without sound
Making documents image-only
Turning on captions for videos and online meetings
check.why: Captions help many people, including people with hearing disabilities.

check.q: You are not sure how to refer to a new colleague. What would you do?
options: Guess and hope
Ask politely or use their name
Avoid talking to them
Ask another coworker to find out
check.why: When unsure, ask politely or just use their name.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Responding to exclusion or harassment
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Respond quickly and properly when someone is excluded, mistreated or harassed.
This lesson builds toward: When someone reports or you see exclusion or harassment, you will list the steps you will follow, who you will tell and where the official rules are, acting right away and protecting the person from retaliation.
Exclusion can be small: always leaving one person off the lunch invite, ignoring their ideas, or making jokes at their expense. Harassment is more serious: unwelcome conduct based on things like race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability or genetic information. As a leader, you cannot ignore either.
If you see it, act. Interrupt calmly in the moment ("That's not okay here"), then talk privately with the person affected and ask what they need. If someone tells you about harassment, listen, thank them, do not promise to keep it secret if your policy requires you to report it, write down what they said, and report it to HR or the person named in your policy right away.
Protect people from retaliation: no one should be punished for raising a concern or helping an investigation. In the US, the EEOC explains harassment, retaliation and how to file a complaint on eeoc.gov. If someone is in danger, call emergency services. Get advice from HR or an employment lawyer on your legal duties.
Step by step:
- If you see it, interrupt calmly in the moment.
- Talk privately with the person affected and ask what they need.
- If someone reports harassment: listen, thank them, write it down.
- Don't promise secrecy if your policy says you must report.
- Report to HR or the person named in your policy right away.
- Make sure no one is punished for speaking up.
Words to know:
- Harassment: unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic, serious or frequent enough to make work hostile.
- Retaliation: punishing someone for complaining about discrimination or helping an investigation.
- Bystander: a person who sees something wrong happen to someone else.
Official sources:
- EEOC: Employers (harassment, retaliation, accommodation)
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page inclusion habits plan. Include one belonging habit, one bias check, three fair hiring or promotion habits, a meeting routine, one accessibility fix, and the steps you will follow if someone reports exclusion or harassment, with who you will tell and where to check the rules.
You can now respond to exclusion or harassment quickly and properly, protect people who speak up, and know where to check your legal duties.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Belonging habit No habit, or a one-time event. One belonging habit the leader can repeat. Says how they will ask the team whether it helps. Bias check No check, or the check comes after the decision. A bias check used on a real decision: criteria first, reasons written down. Also gets a second opinion on the decision. Fair hiring or promotion Fewer than three habits, or habits not tied to the job. Three habits that judge everyone by the same job-related standards. Includes structured interview questions scored by more than one person. Meetings and accessibility No meeting routine or no accessibility improvement. A meeting routine that gives every voice a turn, and one accessibility improvement. Says how they will step in on interruptions or ideas taken without credit. Response steps Steps are missing, or the plan promises to keep a report secret against policy. Steps for a report of exclusion or harassment, who they will tell and where the official rules are. Includes protecting the person from retaliation and calling emergency services if someone is in danger. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is an example of small, everyday exclusion?
options: Always leaving one person off the lunch invite
Giving clear deadlines
Holding one-on-ones
Sharing news with everyone at once
check.why: Exclusion can be small but repeated, and leaders should not ignore it.

check.q: Someone who raised a concern is suddenly left off a project by their manager. What is this a sign of?
options: Normal scheduling
Fair promotion
Possible retaliation, which you must stop
A structured interview
check.why: No one should be punished for raising a concern.
